pages.text: Inside the domed theatre of the Ghana Planetarium in Accra, fourteen-year-old Kofi adjusted his glasses as a glowing river of stars arched overhead. ‘Look toward the constellation Sagittarius,’ said astrophysicist Dr Afia Boateng. ‘Right at the centre of our Milky Way galaxy hides an invisible giant four million times more massive than our Sun.’
sentences: Inside the domed theatre of the Ghana Planetarium in Accra, fourteen-year-old Kofi adjusted his glasses as a glowing river of stars arched overhead.
‘Look toward the constellation Sagittarius,’ said astrophysicist Dr Afia Boateng.
‘Right at the centre of our Milky Way galaxy hides an invisible giant four million times more massive than our Sun.’
pages.alt: Inside the planetarium dome in Accra, Kofi and Adwoa look up with Dr Afia Boateng at the glowing band of the Milky Way.

pages.text: ‘You mean a supermassive black hole!’ said Kofi, opening his sketchbook. ‘In movies, black holes act like giant cosmic vacuum cleaners that roam through space and suck in everything. Will the one in our galaxy swallow the Earth one day?’
sentences: ‘You mean a supermassive black hole!’ said Kofi, opening his sketchbook.
‘In movies, black holes act like giant cosmic vacuum cleaners that roam through space and suck in everything.
Will the one in our galaxy swallow the Earth one day?’
pages.alt: Kofi holds his astronomy sketchbook and asks Dr Afia a question while Adwoa listens.

pages.text: Dr Afia chuckled and shook her head. ‘That is Hollywood fiction, Kofi! A black hole is not a vacuum cleaner. Far away from it, its gravity pulls just like any normal star of the same mass. If our Sun were magically squeezed into a black hole of the exact same mass today, Earth would not get sucked in at all. We would keep orbiting in the exact same path, though we would freeze without sunlight!’
sentences: Dr Afia chuckled and shook her head.
‘That is Hollywood fiction, Kofi!
A black hole is not a vacuum cleaner.
Far away from it, its gravity pulls just like any normal star of the same mass.
If our Sun were magically squeezed into a black hole of the exact same mass today, Earth would not get sucked in at all.
We would keep orbiting in the exact same path, though we would freeze without sunlight!’
pages.alt: Dr Afia holds up a model of the yellow Sun and a tiny dark sphere in the centre of Earth’s unchanged orbit.

pages.text: ‘Then what makes a black hole so special?’ asked Adwoa. ‘Extreme density,’ replied Dr Afia. ‘Gravity depends on both mass and distance. When a giant star many times heavier than our Sun runs out of nuclear fuel, its core collapses under its own weight, cramming enormous mass into a tiny space.’
sentences: ‘Then what makes a black hole so special?’ asked Adwoa.
‘Extreme density,’ replied Dr Afia.
‘Gravity depends on both mass and distance.
When a giant star many times heavier than our Sun runs out of nuclear fuel, its core collapses under its own weight, cramming enormous mass into a tiny space.’
pages.alt: On the planetarium dome, a massive blue star exhausts its fuel and its core collapses inward under gravity.

pages.text: Dr Afia picked up a tennis ball. ‘On Earth, if you throw this ball upward at eleven kilometres per second, it escapes Earth’s gravity into space. We call that escape velocity. The more mass you pack into a smaller radius, the faster the escape velocity becomes.’
sentences: Dr Afia picked up a tennis ball.
‘On Earth, if you throw this ball upward at eleven kilometres per second, it escapes Earth’s gravity into space.
We call that escape velocity.
The more mass you pack into a smaller radius, the faster the escape velocity becomes.’
pages.alt: Dr Afia tosses a yellow tennis ball upward in her hand as Kofi and Adwoa watch its arc.

pages.text: ‘Around a black hole,’ Dr Afia continued, ‘gravity becomes so intense close to the centre that the escape velocity exceeds three hundred thousand kilometres per second, the speed of light! Since nothing in the universe can travel faster than light, nothing that crosses that boundary can ever escape. Scientists call that one-way boundary the event horizon.’
sentences: ‘Around a black hole,’ Dr Afia continued, ‘gravity becomes so intense close to the centre that the escape velocity exceeds three hundred thousand kilometres per second, the speed of light!
Since nothing in the universe can travel faster than light, nothing that crosses that boundary can ever escape.
Scientists call that one-way boundary the event horizon.’
pages.alt: A diagram on the dome shows light rays bending near a black hole and unable to escape inside the spherical event horizon.

pages.text: ‘Note that the event horizon is not a solid wall you could knock on,’ Dr Afia added, stretching a dark elastic cloth over a round hoop and placing a heavy brass weight in the middle. ‘According to Albert Einstein’s general relativity, mass curves the fabric of spacetime. Near a black hole, spacetime is curved so steeply that all paths inside the event horizon lead inward.’
sentences: ‘Note that the event horizon is not a solid wall you could knock on,’ Dr Afia added, stretching a dark elastic cloth over a round hoop and placing a heavy brass weight in the middle.
‘According to Albert Einstein’s general relativity, mass curves the fabric of spacetime.
Near a black hole, spacetime is curved so steeply that all paths inside the event horizon lead inward.’
pages.alt: Dr Afia places a heavy brass sphere on a stretched dark fabric hoop while Kofi rolls a small marble along the curved dip.

pages.text: Adwoa frowned thoughtfully. ‘If no light can escape from inside the event horizon, then a black hole is completely dark. How can astronomers prove it is really there instead of just making it up?’ ‘Brilliant question!’ said Dr Afia. ‘We detect an invisible giant by observing how it affects the universe around it.’
sentences: Adwoa frowned thoughtfully.
‘If no light can escape from inside the event horizon, then a black hole is completely dark.
How can astronomers prove it is really there instead of just making it up?’ ‘Brilliant question!’ said Dr Afia.
‘We detect an invisible giant by observing how it affects the universe around it.’
pages.alt: Adwoa raises her hand with a thoughtful expression while Dr Afia points to four evidence panels on the screen.

pages.text: ‘First,’ said Dr Afia, ‘astronomers tracked stars near the centre of our Milky Way for over twenty-five years. One star, called S2, whips around an completely empty-looking spot at thousands of kilometres per second! Using Kepler’s and Newton’s laws, the star’s orbit proves that four million solar masses are concentrated inside that tiny dark region, which we call Sagittarius A-Star.’
sentences: ‘First,’ said Dr Afia, ‘astronomers tracked stars near the centre of our Milky Way for over twenty-five years.
One star, called S2, whips around an completely empty-looking spot at thousands of kilometres per second!
Using Kepler’s and Newton’s laws, the star’s orbit proves that four million solar masses are concentrated inside that tiny dark region, which we call Sagittarius A-Star.’
pages.alt: The dome displays elliptical golden star orbits looping tightly around an unseen central point in the Milky Way.

pages.text: ‘Second,’ she continued, ‘when gas and dust spiral toward a black hole, friction heats the swirling accretion disk to millions of degrees, making it shine fiercely in X-rays before it crosses the event horizon. Third, when two black holes collide, they send ripples through spacetime called gravitational waves, first detected in twenty fifteen!’
sentences: ‘Second,’ she continued, ‘when gas and dust spiral toward a black hole, friction heats the swirling accretion disk to millions of degrees, making it shine fiercely in X-rays before it crosses the event horizon.
Third, when two black holes collide, they send ripples through spacetime called gravitational waves, first detected in twenty fifteen!’
pages.alt: Two visual scenes glow side by side: a bright orange swirling accretion disk and blue ripples of gravitational waves from two merging black holes.

pages.text: ‘And in twenty nineteen and twenty twenty-two,’ Dr Afia said proudly, ‘the Event Horizon Telescope linked radio dishes across the globe to capture the first real images of the glowing orange ring of gas framing the dark shadow of M87-Star and our own Milky Way’s Sagittarius A-Star!’ Kofi’s eyes widened at the famous orange-ring photograph.
sentences: ‘And in twenty nineteen and twenty twenty-two,’ Dr Afia said proudly, ‘the Event Horizon Telescope linked radio dishes across the globe to capture the first real images of the glowing orange ring of gas framing the dark shadow of M87-Star and our own Milky Way’s Sagittarius A-Star!’ Kofi’s eyes widened at the famous orange-ring photograph.
pages.alt: Kofi and Adwoa admire the famous glowing orange ring image of a supermassive black hole’s shadow on the planetarium screen.

pages.text: ‘Do scientists know what happens at the very centre inside a black hole?’ asked Kofi. ‘Not yet!’ said Dr Afia honestly. ‘General relativity predicts a point of infinite density, while quantum mechanics rules the tiniest particles. Physicists are still searching for a unified theory of quantum gravity to explain what truly happens deep inside, and how information escapes. Perhaps you two will help solve it!’ The end.

pages.alt: Outside the Ghana Planetarium at twilight, Kofi and Adwoa smile with Dr Afia under the first evening stars.

activities.question: What would happen to Earth’s orbit if the Sun were suddenly replaced by a black hole of the exact same mass?
options: Earth would keep orbiting in the exact same path around it
Earth would be sucked into the centre like a vacuum cleaner
Earth would fly straight out of the Milky Way galaxy
The black hole would chase the planets around the solar system
activities.explanation: Black holes are not cosmic vacuum cleaners; at the same distance, a black hole exerts the same gravitational pull as a star of equal mass.

activities.definition: In astronomy, the event horizon is the one-way boundary around a black hole where escape velocity equals the speed of light.
distractors: A solid iron shell built around a star
The bright surface of a normal yellow star

activities.question: Which of these is real observational evidence that astronomers use to detect and study black holes?
options: Star orbits, X-rays from accretion disks, gravitational waves and EHT images
Sending astronauts with flashlights inside the event horizon and back
Listening to sound waves travelling through the vacuum of space
Ancient legends written before telescopes existed
activities.explanation: Astronomers combine stellar orbit tracking, X-ray observations of accretion disks, gravitational-wave detectors (LIGO/Virgo), and the Event Horizon Telescope.

activities.question: Why do physicists say that what happens at the very centre inside a black hole is still an unresolved question?
options: Scientists still need a unified theory combining relativity and quantum physics
Astronomers have never detected any black holes in space
Telescopes cannot see the Milky Way galaxy from Earth
Gravity stops working outside the solar system
activities.explanation: General relativity and quantum mechanics clash at extreme scales inside the event horizon, making quantum gravity an active frontier of research.

activities.prompt: In the stretched-cloth model, what happens when you roll a marble fast near the outer edge versus rolling it slowly right toward the steep dip?
Put these steps in order showing how a stellar-mass black hole forms and is detected.
items: A massive star exhausts its nuclear fuel after millions of years.
The star’s core collapses under gravity into an extremely dense region.
An event horizon forms where escape velocity exceeds light speed.
Astronomers detect it via star orbits, X-rays or gravitational waves.

activities.prompt: How do you feel when a scientist admits "We do not know yet" and explains how researchers are working to find out?

glossary.definition: The universal force of attraction between all objects with mass or energy.
How much mass is packed into a given volume of space.
Speed in a given direction; escape velocity is the speed needed to break free from gravity.
In "event horizon", the boundary around a black hole beyond which light cannot escape.
The four-dimensional fabric combining three dimensions of space and one dimension of time.
The coming together of gas and matter under gravity into a swirling disk around a massive object.
